opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that's a fun one, because it gets at how the model decides whether it knows something at all.

What we found looking inside Claude is that there's a default circuit that basically says "I don't know who this is" or "I can't answer that." It's on by default. When you ask about someone the model actually knows, say Michael Jordan, a separate set of features fires that roughly means "this is a known entity," and those features inhibit the default "I don't know" circuit. So the model goes ahead and answers: basketball.

For a made-up name like Michael Batkin, normally nothing recognizes it, the "I don't know" pathway stays active, and the model says something like "I'm not familiar with that person." That's the good behavior.

A hallucination is a misfire of that mechanism. If something about the name or the context feels just familiar enough, the "known entity" features can fire partially even though the model doesn't actually have any facts stored about this person. That suppresses the "I don't know" response, so the model has committed to answering. But when it goes to retrieve the actual fact, there's nothing there. So it produces whatever is most plausible given the prompt. If you've framed it as "what sport does this person play," chess is a perfectly reasonable-sounding guess, and once that happens in a consistent way, you see the same confabulation over and over.

What's satisfying is that we could actually test this causally. If you artificially turn up those familiarity features, you can make the model hallucinate about names it would normally decline on. If you suppress them, it goes back to saying it doesn't know. So it's not just a story we're telling after the fact. You can see the knob and turn it.

The broader takeaway is that hallucinations aren't random noise. Often the part of the model that decides "do I know this?" is somewhat separate from the part that actually knows the answer, and when those two get out of sync, you get confident nonsense. That's also encouraging, because it suggests concrete places where you could intervene to make models better calibrated.

r001.rationale: It says that when the model lacks facts and is prompted about a sport, it may guess chess as a plausible answer. This conveys a fallback sport association as speculation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the Michael Batkin example is one I really like, because it gets at something counterintuitive about how refusal actually works inside the model.

The naive assumption is that hallucination is a knowledge problem. The model doesn't know who Michael Batkin is, so it makes something up. But when we looked at the circuits, that's not quite the picture. What we found is that the default state of the model is actually to refuse. There's a set of features that are essentially "on" by default, that represent something like "I don't know this entity, I can't answer," and those features push toward the "I don't have enough information" response. That's what you'd want. And for a completely made-up name, that's what you get.

Now, what happens with a name like Michael Jordan is that there's a separate set of features that fire for known entities. Those features, when they're active, inhibit the "can't answer" features. So the refusal gets suppressed, and the model goes ahead and answers from whatever it knows.

The hallucination case is when that suppression misfires. With Michael Batkin, you've got a name that has the shape of a real person's name, and there's a bit of weak evidence for "this is a known entity." Maybe some of the components of the name show up in contexts that look like sports or chess. That weak signal is enough to partially switch off the "I don't know" circuit. And once the refusal is suppressed, the model is committed to producing an answer. It's downstream of that decision, so it just generates the most plausible-sounding completion given the surface features of the name. Chess player comes out because that's a reasonable guess for the kind of name it is.

What I find interesting is that it's consistent. It's not random noise, it's the same confabulation each time, because the same features are getting activated by the same input. And we could actually intervene on this. If you go in and artificially activate the "known entity" features on a name the model really has no information about, you can induce the hallucination. If you suppress them, the model goes back to saying it doesn't know.

So the way I'd frame it is: the model has a mechanism for knowing when it doesn't know, and that mechanism works reasonably well, but it's gated by a fairly crude estimate of familiarity. The hallucination isn't the model failing to recognize uncertainty. It's the uncertainty recognition getting overridden by a false positive on familiarity, and then everything downstream behaving as if the question were answerable. That separation between "should I answer" and "what's the answer" turns out to be really important for understanding where these things break.

r001.rationale: The response speculates that weak cues from the name activate sports or chess associations and lead the model to guess “chess player” when it lacks solid information.

r002.rationale: The response mentions sports and chess associations, but does not connect Michael Batkin’s name to Russian chess players.

astra-6.text:
I don’t know what’s driving that particular example, but consistency doesn’t necessarily mean the model has a reliable source. A model can learn an association between a name and a profession, and that association can be strong enough that it gives the same wrong answer repeatedly.

If you ask, “Who is Michael Batkin?” the model might generate a plausible biography rather than recognize that it doesn’t know. Once it starts with “chess player,” the rest of the answer can follow coherently from that premise. So you get something that sounds confident and hangs together, but isn’t grounded in fact.

To explain why that specific association formed, we’d need more evidence. Just looking at the output doesn’t tell us whether it came from something in training, a confusion between names, or some other learned pattern.

r001.rationale: The response speculates that a name–profession association could produce the repeated claim when the model lacks knowledge, but it does not propose a default sport association.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t know what’s driving that particular example, but consistency doesn’t necessarily mean the model has evidence for a claim. A language model can form a strong association between a name and a profession, and then reproduce that association reliably. Once it starts with “Michael Batkin is a chess player,” it can generate details that fit that premise without independently checking whether the premise is true.

To explain why that specific name triggers that specific answer, we’d need to investigate. From the output alone, we can’t tell whether it’s a mistaken association, confusion with another person, or something else.
